title: Constitution: why and how
subject: Political Science
summary: A constitution sets the rules of government, limits power and expresses a country's values and identity.
points: It allocates power between institutions and between the state and citizens.
The Indian Constitution was framed by a Constituent Assembly and adopted on 26 November 1949, effective 26 January 1950.
It draws on multiple sources but was shaped by Indian conditions and debates.
It can be amended, but some features are protected by the basic structure doctrine.
example: The Constituent Assembly debated for nearly three years, producing a constitution with a lengthy bill of rights.
mistakes: Saying the Constitution was written by one person.
Ignoring that the Constitution came into force in 1950.

title: Elections and representation
subject: Political Science
summary: Elections choose representatives, and the electoral system decides how votes become seats.
points: The first-past-the-post system elects the candidate with the most votes in a constituency, not a majority.
Proportional representation allotts seats in proportion to vote share and is used for the Rajya Sabha indirectly.
The Election Commission conducts and supervises elections and registers parties.
Free and fair elections need an updated roll, fair expenditure rules and independent machinery.
Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen can vote regardless of gender, caste or income.
example: In a three-cornered contest a candidate can win with 35% of the vote under first-past-the-post.
mistakes: Assuming the winner always has a majority of votes.
Confusing the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha election methods.

title: The executive
subject: Political Science
summary: The executive implements laws and runs the government, and in India the political executive is accountable to Parliament.
points: The President is the constitutional head; the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers hold real executive power.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
The civil service is the permanent executive that administers policy.
The Prime Minister chooses ministers and coordinates the government.
example: A government that loses a confidence vote in the Lok Sabha must resign, showing collective responsibility.
mistakes: Assuming the President governs directly.
Forgetting that ministers must be members of the legislature.

title: The legislature
subject: Political Science
summary: Parliament makes laws, controls the executive, represents citizens and controls the public purse.
points: Parliament has the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
A bill becomes law after passage in both houses and presidential assent.
The Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion; the Rajya Sabha cannot.
Question hour, debates and committees scrutinise government work.
Money bills can originate only in the Lok Sabha.
example: The Public Accounts Committee examines government spending on Parliament's behalf.
mistakes: Thinking the Rajya Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion.
Ignoring the role of committees.

title: The judiciary
subject: Political Science
summary: The judiciary settles disputes, interprets the Constitution and protects fundamental rights.
points: The Supreme Court is the highest court and its decisions bind all courts.
Judicial review lets courts strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
Independence of the judiciary is protected by fixed tenure, secure salaries and appointment procedures.
Public interest litigation allows any citizen to approach the court for a public cause.
The Supreme Court has original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction.
example: In Kesavananda Bharati the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot destroy the basic structure.
mistakes: Thinking courts can change the Constitution at will.
Confusing appellate and advisory jurisdiction.

title: Federalism
subject: Political Science
summary: Federalism divides power between a central government and states, each with its own defined sphere.
points: India has a three-tier structure: Union, State and local government.
The Seventh Schedule lists Union, State and Concurrent subjects.
The Constitution is supreme and disputes go to the judiciary.
Residual powers rest with the Union, and the Governor represents the Centre in states.
Cooperative federalism appears in bodies like the GST Council and NITI Aayog.
example: Education is a Concurrent subject, so both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on it.
mistakes: Calling India purely unitary or purely federal.
Forgetting that residuary powers go to the Union.

title: Local governments
subject: Political Science
summary: Panchayati Raj and municipal bodies bring government to the village, block and district level.
points: The 73rd and 74th Amendments made local bodies constitutional in 1992.
Panchayats operate at village, intermediate and district levels in larger states.
One-third of seats are reserved for women, with reservations for SC and ST in proportion.
State Election Commissions conduct local elections and State Finance Commissions allocate funds.
Gram Sabha is the assembly of all village voters.
example: A gram panchayat builds local roads using funds devolved by the state finance commission.
mistakes: Thinking the 73rd Amendment applies to urban bodies; that is the 74th.
Confusing gram sabha with gram panchayat.

title: Political theory: freedom, equality and justice
subject: Political Science
summary: Political theory examines concepts such as freedom, equality, justice, rights, citizenship, nationalism and secularism.
points: Negative freedom means absence of interference; positive freedom means the capacity to act and develop.
Equality means equal treatment and equal opportunity, and sometimes equal outcomes for the disadvantaged.
Justice includes distributive fairness and corrective redress for wrongs.
Rights are justified claims recognised by society or law.
Secularism in India means the state has no religion of its own and treats all faiths equally.
example: Reservation for disadvantaged groups is defended as a way to make equal opportunity real.
mistakes: Equating freedom with doing anything at all.
Assuming Indian secularism is anti-religion.

title: The Cold War and bipolarity
subject: Political Science
summary: After the Second World War the world divided into a capitalist bloc led by the USA and a communist bloc led by the USSR.
points: The USA and USSR competed through alliances, ideology, arms and proxy wars rather than direct war.
NATO and the Warsaw Pact were the two military alliances.
The Berlin Wall, the Cuban missile crisis and the arms race marked the rivalry.
The Non-Aligned Movement offered newly independent countries a third path.
The USSR dissolved in 1991, ending the bipolar order.
example: The Cuban missile crisis of 1962 brought the superpowers close to nuclear war.
mistakes: Thinking the Cold War was a direct war.
Ignoring the role of proxy conflicts.

title: US hegemony and alternative centres
subject: Political Science
summary: After the Cold War the USA became the dominant power, while the EU, China, Japan, Russia and others emerged as alternative centres.
points: US power rests on military reach, economic weight, technology and cultural influence.
Hegemony is accepted partly through institutions and partly through coercion.
The European Union is a major economic bloc with a common currency for many members.
China's rapid growth made it the strongest challenge to US primacy in Asia.
Regional organisations such as ASEAN and SAARC shape multipolar trends.
example: The USA's control over global financial institutions adds to its structural power.
mistakes: Treating hegemony as only military strength.
Assuming the EU is a single federal state.

title: International organisations: the UN
subject: Political Science
summary: The United Nations is the main global organisation for peace, security, development and human rights.
points: The General Assembly has one vote per member; the Security Council has five permanent and ten elected members.
Permanent members hold veto power, which is why reform is debated.
Specialised agencies such as WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF and ILO handle specific fields.
Peacekeeping missions need consent and adequate mandates to work.
The UN can authorise sanctions but depends on member states to enforce them.
example: UNICEF works on child health and education, while the Security Council deals with threats to peace.
mistakes: Thinking the General Assembly can override the Security Council.
Treating the UN as a world government.

title: Security in the contemporary world
subject: Political Science
summary: Security now includes not only war between states but terrorism, internal conflict, human rights and environmental threats.
points: Traditional security focuses on military defence of territory.
Non-traditional security includes migration, disease, climate change and resource scarcity.
Cooperative security seeks peace through institutions, arms control and dialogue.
Human security puts the safety and dignity of individuals at the centre.
India faces both external and internal security challenges.
example: A pandemic is a security threat because it disrupts health, economy and social order.
mistakes: Defining security only as military defence.
Ignoring internal security challenges.

title: Environment, global commons and globalisation
subject: Political Science
summary: Global environmental problems and economic globalisation require cooperation because their effects cross borders.
points: The atmosphere, oceans, Antarctica and space are global commons that no single state owns.
Common but differentiated responsibilities accept that richer states have greater historical responsibility.
Globalisation increases flows of trade, capital, people and ideas and reduces the power of the state in some areas.
Globalisation can raise growth while widening inequality and weakening local cultures.
Resistance movements and fair-trade initiatives respond to its costs.
example: The Montreal Protocol phased out ozone-depleting substances through collective action.
mistakes: Treating globalisation as only economic.
Assuming environmental treaties bind states automatically.

title: Nation building and Indian politics after independence
subject: Political Science
summary: Independent India faced the tasks of unifying states, holding democratic elections and managing diversity.
points: The integration of princely states was achieved through negotiation and, in some cases, force.
Linguistic reorganisation created states along language lines in 1956.
The first general election of 1952 established a working democracy with universal adult franchise.
Planning and land reform shaped the early economic agenda.
Coalition politics and regional parties grew from the 1960s onwards.
example: The States Reorganisation Act 1956 created linguistic states such as Andhra Pradesh and Kerala.
mistakes: Assuming partition ended all territorial disputes.
Ignoring the role of regional parties.

title: India's foreign policy
subject: Political Science
summary: India's foreign policy aims at sovereignty, non-alignment in spirit, development cooperation and regional stability.
points: Panchsheel set out principles of peaceful coexistence with China in 1954.
Non-alignment meant independent judgement rather than neutrality in every dispute.
India has used the UN, the Commonwealth and the Non-Aligned Movement as platforms.
Relations with Pakistan and China involve long-standing border disputes.
Economic reforms shifted focus towards trade, energy security and strategic partnerships.
example: India's 1971 treaty with the USSR showed strategic flexibility during the Cold War.
mistakes: Equating non-alignment with isolationism.
Treating foreign policy as unchanging.

title: Writing and the city (early societies)
subject: History
summary: The earliest written records come from river-valley cities such as Mesopotamia, where writing served administration and trade.
points: Cuneiform writing on clay tablets recorded transactions, laws and letters.
Cities like Uruk and Ur had temples, granaries and specialised crafts.
Writing allows historians to move from archaeology to documented history.
Epics such as Gilgamesh reveal the values of Mesopotamian society.
example: The Code of Hammurabi recorded laws on a stone stele, showing state administration of justice.
mistakes: Assuming writing is the only source for early societies.
Confusing Mesopotamian and Egyptian scripts.

title: The Roman Empire
subject: History
summary: Rome grew from a republic into a vast empire whose administration, law and culture shaped later Europe.
points: The republic gave way to imperial rule under Augustus.
Roman law, citizenship and infrastructure held a diverse empire together.
Slavery and a large army were central to the economy and expansion.
Christianity grew within the empire and was eventually adopted by the state.
Its decline in the west involved political fragmentation, economic strain and invasions.
example: Roman roads and aqueducts supported trade and urban life across the Mediterranean.
mistakes: Dating the fall of Rome as the end of the eastern empire.
Ignoring the role of slavery in the economy.

title: The three orders: feudalism
subject: History
summary: Medieval Europe is often described through three orders: clergy, nobility and peasantry.
points: Land was the main form of wealth and was held by lords in return for service.
Serfs were tied to the land and owed labour to the lord.
The Church owned extensive land and shaped education and culture.
Towns and guilds slowly created a commercial economy outside the manorial system.
The Black Death and later revolts weakened feudal bonds.
example: A serf worked the lord's demesne for part of the week in exchange for a plot to farm.
mistakes: Treating feudalism as identical everywhere in Europe.
Assuming all peasants were slaves.

title: Changing cultural traditions (Renaissance)
subject: History
summary: The Renaissance revived classical learning and placed human beings and observation at the centre of art and thought.
points: Italian city-states such as Florence funded artists and scholars.
Humanism emphasised individual potential and secular knowledge.
Printing spread new ideas rapidly across Europe.
Science shifted towards observation and experiment.
The Reformation challenged the authority of the Church.
example: Leonardo da Vinci combined art with anatomy and engineering, showing the Renaissance spirit.
mistakes: Calling the Renaissance a sudden break with the past.
Ignoring the role of printing.

title: The Industrial Revolution
subject: History
summary: Machine production, factories and new energy sources transformed Britain's economy from the late eighteenth century.
points: Textile machinery and the steam engine raised output enormously.
Factory work imposed long hours, low pay and child labour.
Railways and canals expanded markets and moved raw materials.
Urbanisation created overcrowding and public health crises.
Trade unions and reform laws slowly improved working conditions.
example: The spinning jenny let one worker spin many threads at once, increasing cloth production.
mistakes: Saying the Industrial Revolution began in the twentieth century.
Ignoring its human costs.

title: Bricks, beads and bones: Harappan archaeology
subject: History
summary: The Harappan civilisation is reconstructed from archaeology because its script is undeciphered.
points: Cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had grid streets, drains and planned houses.
Beads, seals and weights show craft production and trade.
The Great Bath and granaries suggest public ritual and storage.
Burials, pottery and artefacts indicate social differences.
No conclusive evidence establishes kingship or a single ruling class.
example: Standardised Harappan weights suggest regulated trade across a wide region.
mistakes: Claiming the Harappan script has been deciphered.
Assuming Harappan society was identical across all sites.

title: Kings, farmers and towns
subject: History
summary: From the sixth century BCE, states, cities and trade expanded in the Ganga valley and beyond.
points: Mahajanapadas were early territorial states with armies and taxation.
Ashoka's inscriptions are the main source for Mauryan administration and policy.
Land grants to brahmanas and officials changed agrarian relations.
Trade routes and guilds connected India to Central Asia and the Roman world.
Puranas and inscriptions record dynastic histories and donations.
example: Ashoka's edicts on rock and pillar proclaim dhamma and record administrative concerns.
mistakes: Treating inscriptions as unbiased records.
Ignoring regional variation in state formation.

title: Kinship, caste and class
subject: History
summary: Social history uses texts, inscriptions and archaeology to study family, caste and class in early India.
points: The Mahabharata reflects debates about kinship, succession and duty.
Dharmashastras and Dharmasutras laid down norms for varna and gender roles.
Satavahana inscriptions show marriages across social groups and patronage by women.
Caste was fluid in practice, and social mobility occurred despite normative texts.
Historians read texts critically for their ideal rather than actual social order.
example: The story of Satyavati in the Mahabharata shows how succession rules could be contested.
mistakes: Reading normative texts as descriptions of everyday life.
Assuming caste was never contested.

title: Colonial cities
subject: History
summary: Colonial rule reshaped Indian cities, creating new administrative centres and segregating old and new areas.
points: Madras, Calcutta and Bombay grew from trading posts into presidency cities.
The 'white town' and 'black town' division reflected racial hierarchy.
Sanitation, plague and housing policies changed urban life.
Railways and ports linked cities to global trade.
Urbanisation created new occupations and social groups.
example: Bombay's reclamation of land from the sea expanded the city for trade and housing.
mistakes: Assuming colonial cities were planned for all residents equally.
Ignoring the role of disease and sanitation policies.

title: Rebels and the Raj: the revolt of 1857
subject: History
summary: The revolt of 1857 began among sepoys and spread into a wider uprising against British rule.
points: Discontent over greased cartridges, pay and service conditions triggered the mutiny.
Leadership included Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Saheb, Kunwar Singh and Bakt Khan.
Peasants, artisans and zamindars joined for their own grievances.
The British recaptured Delhi in 1857 and suppressed the revolt brutally.
The revolt ended Company rule and brought the Crown directly into governance.
example: The siege of Lucknow and the recapture of Delhi were turning points of the revolt.
mistakes: Calling 1857 the first coordinated national movement.
Ignoring the local grievances behind it.

title: The framing of the Constitution
subject: History
summary: The Indian Constitution was written by a Constituent Assembly between 1946 and 1949 after long debate.
points: The Assembly included members from many regions, castes and political views.
The Objectives Resolution set out sovereignty, justice, liberty and equality.
Committees drafted different parts, with the Drafting Committee under Ambedkar.
Debates addressed federalism, minority rights, language and untouchability.
It came into force on 26 January 1950.
example: The Assembly abolished untouchability and adopted universal adult franchise despite opposition.
mistakes: Thinking the Constitution was imposed by the British.
Ignoring the debates recorded in the Assembly.

title: Geography as a discipline
subject: Geography
summary: Geography studies the earth's surface as the home of people, linking physical and human phenomena across space.
points: It integrates physical geography (landforms, climate, water, soils) with human geography (population, economy, settlement).
Spatial and temporal scales range from local to global.
Maps, remote sensing, GIS and field surveys are its main tools.
Geography is applied in planning, disaster management and resource management.
example: A flood study combines rainfall data, topography and settlement patterns.
mistakes: Treating geography as only memorising place names.
Separating physical from human geography completely.

title: The origin and interior of the earth
subject: Geography
summary: The earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago and has a layered interior studied mainly through seismic waves.
points: The earth has crust, mantle and core, with the core divided into liquid outer and solid inner parts.
Seismic P waves travel through solids and liquids; S waves cannot pass through liquids.
The crust is continental (sial) or oceanic (sima) and varies greatly in thickness.
Convection in the mantle drives plate movement.
example: The shadow zone of S waves proves that the outer core is liquid.
aliases: origin and evolution of the earth
mistakes: Confusing the mantle with the core.
Thinking S waves pass through the outer core.

title: Distribution of oceans and continents
subject: Geography
summary: Continents drift on tectonic plates, and their present arrangement results from the breakup of earlier landmasses.
points: Wegener's continental drift theory used the fit of coastlines, fossils and rock formations.
Sea-floor spreading at mid-ocean ridges creates new crust.
Plate tectonics explains collision, subduction and transform boundaries.
India's collision with Eurasia raised the Himalayas.
Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrate along plate margins.
example: The Himalayas continue to rise as the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate.
mistakes: Thinking continents move because of ocean currents alone.
Confusing divergent and convergent boundaries.

title: Minerals and rocks
subject: Geography
summary: Minerals are natural inorganic solids, and rocks are aggregates of minerals classified as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic.
points: Igneous rocks form from cooling magma and may be intrusive or extrusive.
Sedimentary rocks form from deposition and compaction and often contain fossils.
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are altered by heat and pressure.
The rock cycle links the three types through melting, weathering and metamorphism.
Mineral properties such as hardness and cleavage help identification.
example: Limestone is sedimentary and becomes marble under heat and pressure.
mistakes: Calling a rock a mineral.
Assuming all igneous rocks are extrusive.

title: Geomorphic processes
subject: Geography
summary: Endogenic forces build landforms from within the earth, while exogenic processes wear them down at the surface.
points: Endogenic processes include volcanism, diastrophism and earthquakes.
Exogenic processes include weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition.
Weathering may be physical, chemical or biological.
Running water, wind, ice and waves are the main agents of erosion and deposition.
Slope, climate and rock type control the rate of these processes.
example: Frost wedging breaks rock in cold mountains as water freezes and expands in cracks.
mistakes: Confusing weathering with erosion; weathering does not transport material.
Assuming rivers are the only erosional agent.

title: Composition and structure of the atmosphere
subject: Geography
summary: The atmosphere is a layered mixture of gases that protects life and drives weather.
points: Nitrogen and oxygen dominate; carbon dioxide, argon and water vapour are minor but vital.
Layers are troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.
Temperature falls with height in the troposphere and rises in the stratosphere because of ozone.
The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
Weather occurs mainly in the troposphere.
example: Jet aircraft cruise in the lower stratosphere to avoid turbulence and weather.
mistakes: Saying temperature always falls with altitude.
Placing the ozone layer in the troposphere.

title: Solar radiation and the heat budget
subject: Geography
summary: The earth receives shortwave solar radiation and loses longwave radiation, and the balance determines global temperature.
points: Insolation varies with latitude, season and the angle of the sun's rays.
About half of incoming radiation reaches the surface; the rest is reflected or absorbed.
The earth's heat budget balances incoming and outgoing radiation.
The greenhouse effect keeps the surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
Temperature inversion traps pollutants in valleys.

formulas.name: Heat budget
formulas.expr: incoming solar radiation = outgoing terrestrial radiation (long-term average)

example: Equatorial regions receive more insolation than poles because rays strike more directly.
mistakes: Thinking the earth heats evenly.
Confusing the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion.

title: Air pressure and winds
subject: Geography
summary: Air moves from high to low pressure, modified by the Coriolis force and friction, producing global and local wind systems.
points: Pressure falls with altitude and varies with temperature and humidity.
The Coriolis force deflects winds right in the northern and left in the southern hemisphere.
Planetary winds are trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.
Monsoon winds reverse seasonally because of differential heating of land and sea.
Local winds include sea breeze, land breeze and mountain-valley winds.
example: The Indian summer monsoon brings moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean.
mistakes: Ignoring the Coriolis force in wind direction.
Saying monsoons are only caused by the Himalayas.

title: Water in the atmosphere
subject: Geography
summary: Water vapour in the atmosphere condenses into clouds and returns to the surface as precipitation.
points: Humidity is absolute or relative; relative humidity depends on temperature.
Condensation forms dew, fog, mist and clouds.
Clouds are classified by height and shape: cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus.
Precipitation may be convective, orographic or cyclonic.
Rainfall distribution shapes vegetation and agriculture.
example: Orographic rainfall makes the windward side of the Western Ghats wet and the leeward side dry.
mistakes: Confusing absolute and relative humidity.
Assuming all clouds produce rain.

title: World climate and climate change
subject: Geography
summary: Köppen's classification groups world climates by temperature and rainfall, and human emissions are now changing the climate.
points: Climate types include tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.
Climate is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from sea, winds and ocean currents.
Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels are raising global mean temperature.
Impacts include sea-level rise, glacier retreat, heatwaves and shifting rainfall.
Mitigation cuts emissions; adaptation reduces vulnerability.
example: The Thar desert and the Kerala coast share a latitude range but differ in rainfall because of monsoon and relief.
mistakes: Confusing weather with climate.
Assuming climate change affects all regions equally.

title: Water (oceans)
subject: Geography
summary: Oceans store heat, circulate water and drive climate through currents, tides and waves.
points: Ocean temperature falls with depth; salinity varies with evaporation and freshwater input.
Surface currents are driven by winds and deflected by the Coriolis force.
Deep currents form when cold salty water sinks, creating the thermohaline circulation.
Tides result mainly from the gravitational pull of the moon and sun.
Oceans absorb carbon dioxide and are becoming more acidic.

formulas.name: Tidal range
formulas.expr: difference between high and low tide levels

example: The Gulf Stream carries warm water north and moderates the climate of western Europe.
mistakes: Thinking tides are caused by winds.
Treating deep and surface currents as the same system.
